cells.tense: You are here with your hands in the work, and the pull is holding true.
cells.act: govern by knowing what to surrender
cells.ask: Choose what you're growing, and before you touch it again, name the part of it that's finished — then leave that part alone.
cells.core:
The care you bring to growing things is working. You tend what's in reach — a project, a patch of ground, someone's small daily need — with the patience of a person learning how form actually develops. The pull toward what you want is real, and you can tell because the work itself shows you the next move.

What's worth practising now is knowing when a season ends. Not everything living needs more watering. Decide which part of what you're growing is complete, and treat it as complete — stop shaping it, stop checking it. Your hands stay in the work and rest where the work is done. That's what keeps warmth from turning into strain.
cells.sheetLine: You know how to grow things. Now learn when a thing is done.
cells.verb: Learning how things grow by tending them.
cells.place: The place where the pull you steer by is remembered, not arrived.

cells.tense: You are already standing in tomorrow's harvest, deciding how it will taste.
cells.act: dream the next step and take it
cells.ask: Stop planning the whole season. Take the very next step you can take today, without first knowing how it turns out.
cells.core:
The growing has gotten ahead of itself. You can see where this is going so clearly that you start arranging things for a future that hasn't arrived, and care that used to be patient has turned into a push. You're not wrong about the direction — only about the timing. Your hands are trying to hurry what has its own pace.

What's needed is smaller than you think. Instead of building the whole next season in your head, do the one task that's actually here now. Water what's dry, mend what's broken, ask what the ground needs. Do that and stop, without rehearsing how it will go. The future you're bracing for isn't yours to carry yet.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the harvest. That's not the same as standing in it.
cells.verb: Learning how things grow by tending them.
cells.place: The place where the pull you steer by is remembered, not arrived.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door you already walked through, with nothing to grow on the other side.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Pick up something just to see what happens. Keep at it for a week with no goal beyond doing it each day.
cells.core:
Nothing you grow points anywhere right now. The old care is still in your hands — you can feel it — but whatever it was aimed at isn't in view, and nothing new has taken its place. You're not lazy and you're not cold. The pull simply isn't landing anywhere yet.

What rekindles it isn't effort. It's beginning something with no destination — a thing you do because the beginning itself feels alive. Choose something small and yours, not a task for anyone else, and let yourself be a beginner at it. The pull comes back through the starting, not the achieving. Tend it with no name for what it is yet.
cells.sheetLine: Begin something you can't see the end of.
cells.verb: Learning how things grow by tending them.
cells.place: The place where the pull you steer by is remembered, not arrived.

cells.tense: You are growing something in a room you keep saying you only happen to be in.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Notice whatever you're growing that you call someone else's idea or just a habit. Keep it, and put your name on it somewhere you'll see.
cells.core:
You are growing something real, but the way you describe it leaves you out. When people ask why you keep at it, you say it's your job, or it's just what you do, or someone has to. The care is doing its work — the thing is growing — but you don't claim the growing.

The simpler truth is that you chose this. The work is yours, not a role you fell into. So practise owning it without defending it. Next time you tend it, or next time someone asks, say it's yours. Not loudly, not as a speech — just true. The work goes on either way; this only puts you where it's happening.
